sections.title: Archive File 1
sections.text:
A Lupo youth who always wears a smile, yet somehow exudes an oppressive presence.
When Operator Bellone first visited Rhodes Island, a small measure of awkwardness and confusion arose within the HR Department, because we had once written in Operator Vigil's file that Vigil was 'the last leader of Siracusa's Famiglia Bellone.'
Fortunately, we soon got the situation straightened out. According to Operator Bellone, Vigil's father Bernardo—the previous don of the Bellones—had passed away at the time, and Vigil, the heir, had left the old city to devote himself to building Nuova Volsinii. Famiglia Bellone did indeed fall to the brink of collapse for a period, and the power structure within the family disintegrated entirely. Ground down by the other famiglie, the few remaining members of the old Famiglia Bellone could only scrape by. They could neither return to the lives of ordinary people, nor betray the Bellones and throw in with another famiglia. Having seen all this, the young man then known as Demetri Cetaldo resolved to step forward. He took up the Bellone name and gathered everyone who had lost the family's protection under his own care. From that day on, he became the new don of the Bellones.
Based on our current understanding of Siracusa, Bellone's account clearly omits a great many details. For someone who was never the heir to inherit the famiglia—even one already in decline—there would inevitably have been resistance from both inside and outside the family, and his succession could hardly have been as natural and smooth as he describes. But when we asked about those parts, Bellone merely gave a faint smile.
'I grew up inside the famiglia. Its members are family to me, and whatever happens, I could never leave my family to fend for themselves. It really is that simple.' In the end, that was all he said.
It may also be worth mentioning that, at lunch that same day, Bellone likewise ran into Chiave's gang. With his usual cheer, Chiave led his gang in welcoming Bellone's arrival. Bellone seemed somewhat taken aback, but in the end he tolerated Chiave's arm around his shoulder with a smile. The scene felt familiar, and yet it seemed altogether different from the time with Vigil.
'It was only by comparison that I realized how approachable Vigil really is. Bellone had a smile on his face the whole time, but for some reason, I was genuinely worried for Chiave.' recalled an operator who was present.

sections.title: Archive File 2
sections.text:
Famiglia Bellone's foothold in Nuova Volsinii was Saluzzo Vino. Shortly after Demetri Bellone struck his deal with Alberto, Alberto went to prison and Bellone took over the running of Saluzzo Vino. Under his hand the business grew steadily, and after the Red Wine Championship hosted by Kazimierz merchants came to an end, it seized fully half of the local liquor market, gaining enough strength to go toe-to-toe even with the multinational chains from beyond Siracusa.
Beyond the liquor business, the Bellones have invested in no small number of other ventures in Nuova Volsinii. Their momentum has been fierce; although no public figures exist to confirm it, estimates suggest the annual revenue they bring the family already matches that of Saluzzo Vino, and may well exceed it. This does raise certain questions, however. These ventures are concentrated in restaurants, bars, luxury hotels, financial lending, and other fields a famiglia has traditionally invested in as it expands, with little involvement in real industry—which inevitably invites the suspicion that the Bellones may be treading the same old path in Nuova Volsinii. Furthermore, a great many Bellone family members hold posts in these businesses, and within Saluzzo Vino, members of Famiglia Saluzzo remain employed as well. Setting aside the fact that family members occupy the key positions in these enterprises, whether the Saluzzos can sincerely accept Bellone's leadership, whether this will sow trouble within the Bellone family conglomerate, and whether all of the above might further affect the cooperation between Rhodes Island and the Bellones—this string of questions is more worrying still.
Carrying these doubts and concerns, one of our HR operators paid a private visit to Saluzzo Vino.
'Don Demetri? He's a good man!
'Look, we're still called "Saluzzo Vino," aren't we? Don Demetri says the Saluzzos are only working with the Bellones for the time being, so of course we're still Saluzzo men! He even praised our loyalty—said he was glad to work with a family that keeps to tradition the way we do!
'Oh, but we're in Nuova Volsinii now, so Don Demetri says we've got to keep respecting city hall's decisions—do our jobs properly, show up for work, and follow the rules in the New Urban Management Act. Heh, it took some getting used to at first. You know, back in the day, when my terminal rang, my first reaction wasn't to answer it but to check the gun and dagger on me. Now nobody even calls me out to fight. I clock in and out on time every day, go home and eat with my wife and kids—honestly, it feels pretty steady and safe.
'No, no, of course I'm still a member of the famiglia—we're all still waiting for Don Alberto to get out of prison! Come to think of it, I once went to ask Don Demetri whether anything could be done to get Don Alberto out. He said the New Urban Management Act has clear provisions on that sort of thing, so a reduced sentence would be difficult, but he could pull a few strings to make the boss more comfortable inside. On visiting day the other week I went to see Don Alberto—he's got a cell to himself, looked to be in good color, even put on a bit of weight. Thanks to Don Demetri!
'Visits are time-limited, so I couldn't talk with Don Alberto much—I just told him how we've been doing lately. He didn't say anything, but he smiled at the end. I reckon Don Alberto must be grateful to Don Demetri too!'
At this point our HR operator felt that something was not quite right, but looking at the beaming Perro in front of him, he could only follow Alberto's example—smile, and say nothing at all.

sections.title: Archive File 3
sections.text:
We have long known that Demetri Cetaldo was not originally raised to be the don of Famiglia Bellone. His father was once the Bellones' strategist, and died in a clash between famiglie; afterward the young Demetri was taken in by the Bellones and grew up alongside Operator Vigil. Such an arrangement fits our understanding of Siracusan famiglia tradition well: having the family's core members live together is obviously more conducive to cultivating loyalty in the future successors to its important posts.
After his adoption, Demetri quickly accepted his position as Leontuzzo's strategist. He looked after Leontuzzo's daily needs and passed on everything he had mastered—the rules, knowledge, and techniques of famiglia operations, business, and combat—to the boy four years his junior, striving with all his might to raise him into the most perfect leader he could imagine: one who could look after every family member in the famiglia, and guarantee that no member's interests would ever be violated.
This arrangement should have ensured Leontuzzo's smooth succession to the Bellones, but later, old Bernardo brought Lavinia—Operator Penance—into the family, and he came to think differently about the very concept of 'famiglia.' Under Lavinia's influence, Leontuzzo too gradually strayed from the path Demetri had envisioned. This was, of course, a great regret, though it is not hard to understand: for Leontuzzo, the concept of 'family' expanded beyond the members of the famiglia to the people of Nuova Volsinii today, and may one day expand to all Siracusans. And the famiglia's rules, which should have mattered to him above all else, gave way to the law and fairness that Lavinia upheld. That is all.
The above comes from Operator Bellone's own account, which likewise seems to omit a great many details, though we do not intend to press further. Still, regarding Siracusa's so-called famiglia traditions, there is one thing we could not help asking: aside from advising on famiglia operations, is a family's strategist also responsible for looking after the don's daily life?
Bellone did not answer.
Another party involved, however, offered us an answer worth considering—
'A normal strategist wouldn't, no. But Demetri and I grew up together—he's a few years older than me, and he got used to looking after me early on, just as I got used to being looked after. Of course, it's also possible... that guy already had the makings of a don back then. He saw me as family, so he figured taking care of me was simply his duty. "A don ought to look after every one of his family"—he always used to say that to me. And from where I'm standing, he's doing a pretty good job of it now.'

sections.title: Archive File 4
sections.text:
Since the promulgation of the Amendment to the New Urban Management Act, every sector of Nuova Volsinii has been shaken by it. Hardest hit are the foreign companies in the industries the amendment covers; their investors and owners have voiced their dissatisfaction to city hall one after another, but city hall has held firm, and some proprietors have already adjusted their business strategies in line with certain provisions. Local businesses, meanwhile, have applauded it in unison, while remarking that the amendment came far too late. The general public of Nuova Volsinii is broadly in favor, though certain informed observers have pointed out, not without concern, that the amendment in fact amounts to a form of local protectionism—and given Siracusa's long famiglia tradition, they fear the famiglie may rise from the ashes behind the shell of local enterprise.
What changes the amendment will ultimately bring to Nuova Volsinii remains to be seen; this paper will continue to report on the matter.
—The Central News, Overseas Edition

When Bellone finally stood before Signora Sicilia, all he felt within was fear.
That fear did not stem from Signora Sicilia's power—quite the opposite. Standing before her, he could at last see clearly the face he had only ever glimpsed from afar at public occasions: the sagging cheeks, the deep hollows beneath her eyes, the spots on her skin that no cosmetics could fully conceal. It struck him all at once that the legend of Signora Sicilia he had known by heart since childhood had taken place over sixty years ago, and that the woman standing before him now had long since entered her twilight years.
Of course, her eyes were as firm and clear as ever, her movements as composed and forceful, her speech as soft and low as it had always been, carrying an authority no one could refute or defy. All the power of Siracusa was still concentrated in her. And that was precisely why Bellone's fear grew stronger—power was concentrated in her, yet she was not eternal. The order she represented, the deterrence she held over every Siracusan famiglia, even the wariness other nations felt toward Siracusa because of her, would all inevitably scatter and come to nothing once she had aged completely and died. And when that day came, would the famiglie still be willing to sit down in the Grey Hall as they do now, to negotiate and settle their disputes? Would Siracusa sink back into chaos and desolation?
'What becomes of Siracusa after I die is of no concern to me whatsoever.'
So said Signora Sicilia as she climbed the steps of her residence. Her pace was slow, still seemingly steady, yet her hand gripped Bellone's arm far too tightly. And so all Bellone could say was, 'Signora, do not speak of such things. You have many years left.'
'Only children who have never known death and old folk about to walk into it keep the word "death" on their lips—and no one knows my body better than I do.' She smiled. 'The future does not belong to me. Whether it can belong to you—or to all of you—is up to you alone. Your idea is interesting, and by coming to me before you acted, you showed me respect. So go. Go to Nuova Volsinii and give it a try.'
Fear left Bellone unable to reply, yet all the vague notions in his heart before that meeting became clear and resolute in that moment. He had once hoped someone would show him the road, so that he need only obey absolutely. Now, however, he had to become the one who pointed the way and walked it to the end. He would build a new order.
The time left to him, to them, to Siracusa—there is not much of it.

sections.title: Promotion Record
sections.text:
You would step in and help smooth things over between me and Leon? Thank you for the kindness, Doctor, but there is no longer any need for that.
I know he chooses to avoid me while he is on Rhodes Island, and I know that worries you somewhat. But it is only because he does not know how to deal with me in an informal setting. We were once family—brothers who leaned on each other as we grew up, the future don and the strategist who would serve at his side. Now we are business partners, friends who stand as equals. That change leaves him at a loss, and the name 'Bellone' still grates on his ear. All you need to do is give him some time. He will get used to it; he has to. We all have to accept, however reluctantly, the things we cannot change—do we not? After all, Leon chose a different road from mine back then.
No, I do not actually oppose the convictions Lavinia holds to. They are fine convictions; they stand for light and justice, and I fully believe they can lead Nuova Volsinii—and Siracusa—toward a better future. You must understand that I took charge of Leon's education long before Lavinia ever came to the Bellones. The famiglia and Don Bernardo raised me to be a strategist, and I taught Leon everything I knew and everything I believed. I raised him after the image of the ideal don I carried in my heart. Yes, there are minor differences between us, but what he believes in is, in essence, no different from what I believe.
I have walked in the rain far too long, and that is the source of the difference between us. I could never abandon my family—so long as they still call themselves members of the famiglia. In that respect I truly fall short of Don Bernardo and Leon; their resolve and decisiveness are things I do not possess. Even so, I have always believed that I and the Bellones still have the right and the need to exist. Where there is light, there will be shadow, and if you love the fresh air after the rain, you must first endure a long rainy season.
As I am now, I am indeed... still a long way from the ideal don I hold in my heart. But that is fine. The man I was never made it his goal, and the man I am now will not change how he acts on account of it. Leontuzzo Bellone once carried my ideal, but he will not become the don, and I will not become his strategist. I have accepted that. And in the distant future, I can always step back into the strategist's place—so long as someone can prove to me that they can be a better don than I am.
